This paper investigates convergence for a class of stochastic control problems involving discretization when faced with rough data. Convergence is ensured by employing a specific transformation of the time transformation and control parameters, which are not generated via standard methods. Although this approach is more rigid than handling finite data sets, it offers significant practical advantages, most notably the elimination of Monte Carlo sampling error. A key benefit of using this rough data framework is its mathematical tractability; specifically, the continuous time and control elements produce terms that are deterministic and smooth, allowing the resulting approximation algorithms to be substantially simpler to execute. Furthermore, this smooth deterministic setting is well-suited for deriving high-order convergence rates. The method proposed here achieves a third-order rate of convergence even for a broad category of suboptimal stopping problems, an outcome that also applies with ease to the widely used best-fit contract for American puts.

We have conducted a re-examination of cosmic ray directional anisotropy using the full 11.5-year data set collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, covering energies greater than 4 EeV. Employing a novel, streamlined technique for anisotropy analysis, we demonstrate that the findings align closely with prior 7.5-year results. This confirms that the energy dependence of the anisotropy dipole amplitude—observed to rise from roughly 0.02 D$_\perp$ to 0.06 D$_\perp$ in the 10$^{17}$ to 10$^{20}$ eV range—is consistent with extragalactic anisotropy driven by the large-scale structure of the universe at these high energies. Projections for a 20-year analysis are deemed unnecessary for achieving a 2$\sigma$ constraint on such a hypothesis. Additionally, we show that systematic uncertainties in the current 11.5-year results are at least as significant as statistical limitations, suggesting that future expansion of the data archive could yield limited further improvements.

Estimating object pose remains a significant challenge in virtual and augmented reality, particularly when dealing with occlusions and recognition errors. This study introduces Graphical Lasso with Latent Variables (GLLV), a novel extension designed to enhance variable selection and structure learning in high-dimensional, multivariate, Gaussian data sets. Comparing the cost of numerical approaches is vital for selecting algorithms that balance efficiency and accuracy in biomolecular simulations. This study analyzes the algorithmic performance of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MC), Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and Langevin Molecular Dynamics (LM-Dynamics) for simulating alanine dipeptide. By comparing these methods in an isolated system and co-solvent models using explicit and implicit water, we compared their relative costs. We defined cost through wall-clock time required to achieve equivalent statistical precision. Results indicate that, depending on the solvation model, both MC and HM-C outperform Langevin Molecular Dynamics regarding efficiency. Furthermore, Hamiltonian MC matches the sampling accuracy of standard Metropolis-Hastings MC while maintaining comparable computational overhead. Consequently, results suggest MC and HM-C are preferable choices for biomolecular applications.

The Cubanite ($\text{CuFe}_2\text{S}_4$) presents a puzzling anomaly: it exhibits a stable spin-compensated ferromagnetic state despite the presence of FeS subunits that suggest it should be an inverse spinel. To resolve this, we modeled Cubanite using Density Functional Theory (DFT) and discovered that a mismatch in the DFT unit cell's Fe arrangement prevents the spin cancellation required for ferrimagnetism. By engineering a unit cell with the correct Fe configuration, we demonstrated that the switch from the simpler to the complex cell is driven by a drop in magnetic moment, which in turn lowers the energy of the system's Fermi level deep within the valence band. This positioning of the Fermi level stabilizes the observed non-collinear ferromagnetism. Our findings indicate that Cubanite's magnetic ordering arises from antiferromagnetic coupling between iron moments situated on opposite sides of the sulfide layers.

A quantum dot situated within an acoustic cavity constitutes a promising acoustic resonator capable of supporting strong coupling between the dot and point acoustic modes. This capability enables the execution of diverse single-dot protocols, including high-fidelity state initialization, readout, and manipulation. By calibrating the driving laser frequency to align with either the dot's ground-to-excited state transition or its inter-level splitting, operations can be achieved using just one external drive. Specifically, adjusting this frequency allows for selective adjustment of both the coupling strength and detuning between the quantum dot and the acoustic mode independently. Furthermore, varying the drive frequency modulates the characteristics of Rabi oscillations in response to laser excitation. Consequently, a feedback-driven adaptive tuning of the drive laser frequency can automatically establish the conditions required for maximum Rabi frequency or specific detuning values.

A $3\times 3$ honeycomb sub-lattice embedded within a larger honeycomb structure forms a "herringbone" geometry. This paper demonstrates that a $3\times 3$ Hamiltonian, initially proposed for this system, is generalized by additional terms to account for various Hamiltonian perturbations. We analyze the three-band model under such modifications to track changes in the internal dynamics of its three sub-lattice herringbone bands. Specifically, we examine variations in the characteristics of its two Dirac points. Findings reveal that specific perturbations can convert Dirac points into massive Dirac points or shift their positions in momentum space, with one such massive configuration serving as an analogy for graphene under a sub-Davidson (SD) perturbation. We also investigate the "centrifugal" behavior of this system by calculating the spin of relativistic particles with varying momentum orientations and by determining the geffen (Berry) curvature and associated classical force for this band model. Finally, we explore the "centrifugal" effect through these curvature and force metrics and present a theoretical framework for the recently observed massive Dirac point in the honeycomb $3\times 3$ super-lattice known as "herringbone" by manipulating the primary two-band parameters with various perturbative terms in the three-band model. Through this study, we find that the two Dirac points in the system can become massive Dirac points or shift in the $(k_x,k_y)$ space.

A long-standing challenge in soft matter physics involves determining a system's most probable structure, a concept known as the center of mass. This reconfiguration offers a substantial benefit: it allows for an immediate analytical derivation of both the center of mass and its fluctuation spectrum. We validate this method by applying it to two scenarios—an uncharged polymer in free space and an uncharged polymer constrained within a plane. The results demonstrate an exact match with established theories, confirming the accuracy of this streamlined framework. This enhanced model serves as the foundation for investigating charged polymers interacting with interfaces.

Recent advancements in online services, which facilitate interaction across distant geographies, might seem to counteract spatial segregation. Paradoxically, these digital tools may instead reinforce such divides by filtering content based on user location. This positioning-driven filter often promotes the viral spread of misinformation—such as fake news and conspiracy theories—which can exacerbate geographic isolation. To address whether this feedback loop actually occurs, we analyze ten years of WhatsApp data, covering both U.S. and international markets, to map the relationship between conspiracy propagation and changes in the distribution of user residences. Our findings reveal that the release of the "Big Sort" update in January 2015 caused a sharp increase in the geographic segregation of conspiracy-related traffic within the U.S., a trend that persisted for at least a decade. Conversely, similar effects were absent in the international dataset. We further demonstrate that this disassortative mixing of users by geography, triggered by conspiracy contagion, was a primary driver of the observed fragmentation. These results indicate a distinctively American phenomenon that accelerates regional isolation through the very connectivity solutions designed to mitigate it.

The study of the Cauchy problem for the group of unitary quantum fields (UQ) can be reformulated as an optimization challenge, known as Euler-Arnold equations, which facilitates the calculation of trajectories for generic Cauchy data. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing linear complex structures defined on invariant subspaces of the adjoint representation of the group UQ. The resulting linearized Euler-Arnold framework is verified through specific examples, including the free scalar field and the most elementary interaction involving three particles. These findings hold significant implications for the development of numerical methods aimed at solving the Cauchy problem within quantum field theory.

In today's information-rich era, recommendation systems have become indispensable for helping users navigate the vast array of content. A central element of these recommendation systems is collaborative filtering, which learns from user interactions to generate personalized suggestions. However, conventional approaches typically rely on binary feedback (e.g., clicking or not clicking), failing to capture nuanced preferences. To overcome this limitation, Aspect Preference Enhancement (APE) was introduced, allowing for side-agnostic learning by requiring input for a user's preferred item among all available choices. Yet, APE's requirement for explicit item selection creates a significant usability burden. To address this, we propose Contextual Item Re-ranking for Aspect Preference Enhancement (CIR-APE), an approach that automatically re-ranks an user's currently viewed item to the top position in the feed, enabling aspect preference learning without additional feedback. Complementing this, Aspect Preference Learning (ACL) is dynamically adjusted based on the relative positions of other items relative to the user's current choice, utilizing a novel gap-based attention mechanism to derive implicit positive preferences from click behavior. Furthermore, the proposed re-ranking strategy is not static; it dynamically adapts using a contextual item re-ranking module that synthesizes item attributes and user preferences to optimize the presentation order. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets confirm that CIR-APE substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and robustness.

To address this, the authors present a case study examining Google's treatment of the term "unemployment rate" across three distinct interfaces—the main homepage, the Knowledge Graph, and the "Also search for" suggestions. The study reveals that Google employs multiple, varying algorithmic processes which yield different results depending on the user's location and language settings. Furthermore, the findings highlight discrepancies in the sources cited by the "knowledge panel" and "also search for" suggestions, suggesting that such inconsistencies could mislead public sector audiences. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity for public sector practitioners to navigate search engine complexities and to account for potential biases when utilizing information retrieved from platforms like Google.

The proposed TeV-scale muon collider would provide exceptional capabilities for investigating rare particle production processes. This note examines the potential for studying electroweak sphaleron transitions and heavy resonant vector bosons. Additionally, we evaluate the energy reach for probing heavy non-resonant new physics via mixed electroweak and color charges, as well as mechanisms responsible for the non-zero matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Rapid and effective sampling strategies are vital for compressive sensing magnetic resonance imaging (CS-MRI). While linear sampling is computationally efficient, it introduces artifacts and degrades image quality due to its lack of incoherence relative to the undersampled k-space grid. Although recent rCASPR (randomized Compressed Sensing with Autocorrelation and Symmetry PRoperties) sampling methods offer quick acquisition and superior reconstruction by approximating random k-space trajectories, they currently rely on a fixed, stepwise movement between points. This fixed increment mirrors linear sampling, resulting in regular, correlated artifacts within the acquired data. To address this limitation, we propose a rCASPR framework that utilizes variable step sizes to minimize grid autocorrelation and maximize artifact incoherence. By systematically evaluating different step sizes, we demonstrate that the optimal choice minimizes point spread function (PSF) symmetry and lowers contrast loss. Simulations and real experiments confirm that variable step-size rCASPR significantly outperforms both linear and constant-stepsize rCASPR approaches when using the same acquisition parameters.

We introduce a precise, though recursive, strategy to enumerate all pairs within the specific-permutation test sample space. Our method achieves a runtime acceleration of roughly a factor of two compared to the current state-of-the-art exact algorithm for the partition-of-regular-tableau test. Consequently, the proposed exact simulation outperforms stochastic Monte Carlo estimates in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Using a novel comprehensive dataset spanning from 1966 to 2016, this study examines the competitive dynamics within the global shipping industry, specifically analyzing the dissolution of shipping cartels. It investigates how the loss of price rigidity in certain routes contributed to market-wide intensification, triggering competitive pressures that forced freight rate reductions even on other sectors, compelling carriers to engage in aggressive competition through excess capacity. Empirical findings indicate that while the dismantling of tariff agreements on specific routes initially spurred such capacity, the overarching phenomenon of an increasingly competitive industry was ultimately driven by a shift in strategic behavior toward deploying larger vessels. These findings have significant implications for understanding the origins of industry-wide competitive dynamics and form a foundational basis for formulating effective public policies aimed at curbing anti-competitive practices.

We demonstrate that every loom space $X$ admits a loom topological structure linked to it, such that $X$ becomes a topological complex. Furthermore, for each loom space, there exists a loom $\Delta$ where $X$ is homeomorphic to the geometric realization $|\Delta|$, and $\Delta$ is a topological complex representing the space $X$ up to homeomorphism.

Stock price forecasting is a critical concern for investors, driven by the potential for capital appreciation, yet it remains challenging due to the stochastic nature of market dynamics. This research introduces a deep learning framework designed to anticipate stock price trajectories by integrating historical prices with technical indicators. The proposed model employs a two-stage architecture: initially, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) extracts hierarchical features from multi-variable time-series data, followed by a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that models complex inter-variable relationships and performs regression to forecast future values. The study validates the approach using the S&P 500 constituent stocks, evaluating a variety of scenarios with varying look-ahead periods. Empirical results demonstrate the model's robustness and superior performance compared to existing baseline methods. Given its ability to capture nonlinear patterns and causal linkages within historical data, this method offers investors a valuable tool for enhancing decision-making processes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhenghuilin/HCNN.

This study examines the relationship between Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), specifically focusing on the production of Higgs boson pairs. By examining the leading order (LO) and next-to-leading order (NLO) contributions to proton-proton collisions yielding two Higgs bosons, we analyze the correspondence of effective operators. The findings indicate that, for the specific process of pp $\to$ $WW^* \to \text{HH}$, the effective operators governing this channel in HEFT and those at LO in SMEFT share identical structures and coefficients.

The study investigates the forces acting on a cylindrical intruder moving vertically within dense granular assemblies. A high-speed camera tracked the motion of a glass cylinder, allowing the reconstruction of its trajectory and the calculation of drag force via the method of differences. The results indicate that drag is influenced by the intruder's geometry, material density, oscillation amplitude, and velocity. Specifically, the relationship between drag and velocity varies with driving rate: at low rates, the connection remains linear, whereas high driving rates produce a more pronounced non-linear behavior. Furthermore, the study attributes this shift in dynamics to the interplay between the timescale of grain rearrangement and the timescale of intruder displacement. Finally, the paper presents a unified model capable of describing these diverse regimes across varying driving conditions.

This study presents an analysis of the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow ($v_p$) from ALICE collaboration data, specifically examining proton, pion, and various intermediate-mass hadrons within central 7 TeV Pb-Pb collisions. Findings indicate that the shape of the triangular flow as a function of transverse momentum closely resembles that of elliptic flow ($v_2/v_p$) for both protons and identified particles. Building on this resemblance, the work employs a newly developed, efficient numerical technique to derive per-trigger yields for non-single protons and pion/identified mesons in the same $p_T$ interval for Pb-Pb collisions. Furthermore, a detailed comparison is provided between these yields and those obtained from an AliCE data sample covering 36 mb of integrated luminosity in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV.

The LHCb upgrade is designed to enhance the sensitivity of ultra-rare searches for $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$, among other rare processes. These searches are critical for testing the Standard Model and probing potential new physics. This contribution outlines a simulation of these specific rare decays tailored for the LHCb upgrade using the Delphes 2 fast simulation toolkit. Delphes 2 lacks the granularity required to model systematic uncertainties with high precision, making it an essential tool for reducing computational costs during early experimental phases like the upgrade. Delphi 2 is also highly effective for parameterized studies of systematic uncertainties in the analysis of these rare decay modes.

This work introduces and analyzes an enhanced variant of standard FGMRES iterations designed to upgrade numerical solution quality. In each step, the method employs a small nested inner loop to solve the orthogonalization subproblems using GMRES. By selecting an appropriately optimized inner loop restart value, this two-layer structure functions as a fixed-length inner loop repeat scheme. The study establishes a correspondence between the proposed approach and a specific class of restarted GMRES iterations and validates its efficacy through a series of numerical experiments.

Noise commonly found in intraoperative data, such as that from ultrasound, poses a significant challenge in accurately aligning organ models with intraoperative and preoperative datasets. To address this, we propose a noise-robust registration technique that integrates a deformable model with sparse, point-based constraints. In this framework, each constrained point adheres to a specific cross-sectional anatomical shape derived from an atlas, while the elastic properties of the model ensure smooth deformation across the domain to maintain alignment with other points. We validate our approach using sparse ultrasound constraints to register a liver model against both noisy intraoperative ultrasound images and CT scans, comparing results against state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we simulate surgical scenarios involving noisy intraoperative updates and assess how registration accuracy degrades as noise levels increase, comparing these simulations with real-world updates generated by moving an ultrasound probe across an organ surface.

Although self-supervised methods have proven effective in optical flow estimation, flow networks still require ground truth to reach their full potential. We introduce a fully self-supervised approach named Refined-FlowNet (R-FloNet) that eliminates the need for both optical flow and occlusion masks during both training and deployment. While prior self-supervised techniques used stereo disparity as a substitute for flow, we demonstrate that this is suboptimal because stereo matching differs fundamentally from dense flow prediction due to its inherent tolerance for occlusion and depth discontinuities. Consequently, we propose disparity refinement as a crucial step to enhance the accuracy of dense motion estimation. Additionally, we present a novel network architecture designed to jointly learn flow and motion segmentation, leveraging the fact that motion classes are more distinct and easier to identify than specific flow patterns. Extensive experiments confirm that R-FloNet significantly outperforms existing self-supervised methods, particularly in regions of occlusion and depth discontinuity.

Addressing the challenge of training neural networks for safety-critical embedded systems, where reduced power consumption is essential, this study explores the use of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) as a versatile solution. Although SNNs are renowned for their energy efficiency, their widespread adoption has been hindered by the complexity of training them. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a supervised learning algorithm based on the Evolutionary Neuroevolutionary Training (ENET) framework, which is capable of teaching SNNs to execute multi-class classification tasks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed SNN-based method achieves performance levels comparable to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) used in existing studies, while simultaneously delivering significant reductions in both computational cost and power usage.

In this study, we examine the spin-polarized dynamics of non-nucleonic matter within a strong magnetic field, specifically calculating the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter (SPSQM) and meson matter under these conditions. We then analyze the stability of spin-polarized SQQM relative to other forms of nuclear and sub-nuclear matter, incorporating the influence of the magnetic field on the equation of state for spin-polarized SQQM through both the MIT bag model and the percolation model. Finally, we apply the Gibbs jump condition to investigate spin-polarized phase transitions induced by magnetic fields, focusing on the generation, internal structure, and observable characteristics of spin-polarized neutron stars.

We introduce the notion of even-2-factorable (E2F) for cubic graphs, defining it as the property where an "even" 2-factor can be formed such that the graph is partitioned into two "even" 2-factors. We prove that the Haxell-Harper conjecture from 2022 holds true for (5,3)-biregular bipartite graphs. Additionally, we define a new class of graphs, 2-tough, and prove that any graph within this subclass satisfies the E2F property as well.

Application-specific system call filtering (SCF) is vital for securing services like PHP and Python, yet applying SC rules to interpreted languages poses a major challenge. Existing solutions often rely on time-consuming static analysis or fail to generate code that is easy for developers to adopt. To address this, we introduce "timeloops," a straightforward timing-based SC mechanism for interpreted applications. Timeloops automatically generates timing constraints for system calls by leveraging software engineering practices familiar to these communities. It enhances standard interpreter SC handlers with checks that compare the current time against stored limits, rejecting any calls that exceed them. We evaluated timeloops on Python and PHP using three distinct methods: static analysis, manual annotation, and an automated tracing technique we developed. Our findings reveal that the new tracing method offers a highly efficient and practical pathway for populating SC policies across interpreted environments.

This study introduces a data-driven approach utilizing machine learning to efficiently identify missing data caused by data loss or limited sensor fields of view, specifically enabling the detection of data gaps and the localization of previously unseen targets. Unlike traditional methods, this strategy does not require prior assumptions regarding the number of targets, their inherent attributes, or the specific parameters of the sensor's viewing limitations. Instead, it relies on the premise that observable data patterns are influenced by missing data, allowing the model to infer the presence of undetected targets directly from these observations. The core algorithm operates by training a machine learning model on data loss patterns within a controlled environment and subsequently applying it in real-world scenarios to identify areas where data is missing. These inferred gaps are subsequently used to flag potential targets detected by other sensors but absent in their primary feeds. Evaluations conducted both through simulation and using live video feeds demonstrate the method's robustness. Notably, the approach achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity, classifying it as linear ($O(n)$) relative to the number of targets, in contrast to the quadratic ($O(n^2)$) complexity of existing state-of-the-art tracking algorithms.

This study introduces a population dynamics model incorporating an infection phenomenon and an infection-related death rate, with the primary objective of ensuring population extinction. Leveraging an established observability inequality derived in prior work for the related linear backward-in-time system, we analyze the forward problem and demonstrate the existence of a control that guarantees the population reaches extinction. Specifically, population reduction is achieved by applying a non-harvesting control to the infection rate density within an observable subdomain. Furthermore, quantitative estimates for both the control duration required to ensure population collapse and the maximum control magnitude are provided and analyzed.

In the context of football, where a team plays for 90 minutes across three half-court quarters, there are numerous distinct situations, or states, from which a side can kick the ball forward. Naturally, some of these states offer lower potential rewards than others; for instance, committing a foul or causing the ball to go out of play generally provides less value than attempting a shot at goal. Nevertheless, certain defensive strategies, such as committing a deliberate offside trap or intentionally concurring the opponent, are occasionally employed to secure a more favorable state transition. This paper utilizes a decision-theoretic framework to evaluate these defensive choices. By applying the model to data from the 2017/18 Premier League season, the authors analyze the relative merits of various actions—ranging from fouling and throw-ins to shots—in order to quantify their expected in-game value. The findings specifically assess when non-attacking maneuvers outperform aggressive play and offer a granular view of the tactical decisions made by manager Pep Guardiola regarding his Bayern Munich squad. Ultimately, the model serves not only as an analytical tool for understanding game dynamics but also as a supportive resource for coaches and sporting directors during team preparation.

This study introduces a frequency-domain full waveform inversion (FWI) approach that utilizes time-domain wavefields to manage Earth's physical complexity. A key advantage of this method is its compatibility with existing, high-performance parallel solvers typically used in time-domain FWI. To handle the resulting frequency mixing issues, we apply a Grentgen-Arnold operator to compute the frequency-domain Jacobian matrix. Furthermore, to enhance computational efficiency, we propose two strategies for organizing the update gradient: a column-wise approach and a row-wise approach. Assessments through 2D and complex3D simulations demonstrate that this frequency-domain FWI technique achieves performance on par with state-of-the-art methods, while its gradient computation proves significantly more efficient compared to traditional frequency-domain strategies.

We investigate the one-dimensional noisy voter model involving two competing species, where pairs of different species interact to determine the new state of the competitor's species. By analyzing the competition dynamics in asymmetrical settings where at least one pair of noise parameters exists with a ratio not equal to one, we identify three distinct outcomes: the total extinction of both species, the survival of only the stronger species, or the coexistence of both. Furthermore, in the coexistence scenario, we demonstrate that the system's asymptotic behavior falls into one of three categories based on the long-term dynamics: both species' densities converge to fixed values, both densities fluctuate within a range, or the densities exhibit chaotic behavior.

In Data-Centric Device-to-Communication (DED2D) systems, the TFIET (Traffic Feedback and Energy Trade-off) scheme addresses the need to deliver data and energy to end-users. This approach facilitates both data transmission and wireless power transfer, allowing users to retrieve files while simultaneously charging their devices. To optimize performance, the TFIET model jointly determines the resource block allocation for data transfer, the duration of energy transmission, and the bandwidth assigned to each device. The formulation of the Traffic Feedback and Energy Trade-off represents a novel non-convex mixed integer programming challenge. Given the infeasibility of conventional solution methods due to computational complexity as network scale increases, a new subgradient-based iterative method is introduced to achieve near-optimal data rates and energy delivery efficiently. Numerical simulations confirm that this enhanced algorithm significantly outperforms suboptimal benchmarks in achieving a balanced trade-off between data rates and energy supply.

The growing prevalence and mandated increase of remote work have driven a parallel trend toward automating various tasks, including laboratory experimental rigs. Capitalizing on this shift, this paper introduces a fully autonomous system designed to execute and monitor a distributed acoustic beam steering optimization algorithm. Implemented on a budget-friendly, all-computer-architecture known as Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), this system requires no human input while simultaneously providing real-time visualization and comprehensive data logging. We demonstrate its efficacy by self-operated acquisition of an optimization convergence curve for both single and dual laser beams. Consequently, this cost-effective remote solution offers a versatile framework adaptable to other domains that benefit from self-sustaining, optimized operational processes.

The rapid advancement in nanofabrication techniques has enabled the creation of high-resolution nanostructures for electrostatic phase plates (EPPs), which induce phase shifts in electron waves to enhance the contrast of phase images in transmission electron microscopy. This study employs the Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) method to investigate the diffraction patterns generated by various EPP designs. Key parameters such as fill-factor and pixel arrangement are analyzed to determine their impact on probe size and current density. Furthermore, the theoretical framework is extended to assess the performance of super-resolution designs, including a specific case study of a honeycomb pixel layout. These findings offer practical guidance for optimizing EPP configurations and are validated against experimental data and existing literature.

This study examines the orbital stability of one-dimensional solitary waves subjected to a cubic-nonlinear Schrödinger equation in an anharmonic oscillator potential. By applying a perturbation method to the exact pseudo-Dumitrescu operator solutions, we demonstrate that stability is preserved despite the anharmonicity of the potential. Furthermore, utilizing perturbation theory, we derive explicit formulas for the first-order anharmonic corrections regarding both the Hamiltonian and the spatial part of the solitary wave. Orbital stability is further established for both two- and three-dimensional systems under similar nonlinear and potential conditions through these adjusted perturbative approaches.

This paper investigates the Galois module structure of the higher K-groups, denoted as ${\rm{K}}_n(\mathcal{O}_L)^{\rm{ab}}$, associated with $ \mathbb{Q} $-extensions $ L/\mathbb{Q} $ that feature a specific finite non-abelian character $ \psi $. The focus is on the action induced by the additive system of these K-groups relative to the group $ {\rm{Irr}}(\psi) $. The authors examine the relationship between the structure of these K-groups within this module framework and the set of finite non-abelian extensions of $ \mathbb{Q} $ that contain a given wildly ramified extension with specific twist properties.

This paper examines the systematic organization of search strategies for neutral long-lived particles (NLSPs) at high-energy colliders, categorizing methods based on the decaying particle's travel distance before disintegration. We outline representative searches within each decay length regime and conclude by outlining future directions in NLSP search methodology.

Recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) suggest that translation updates can reveal semantic changes. However, examining whether these changes constitute meaningful semantic drift or merely surface-level variations remains difficult. We introduce a unified framework designed to evaluate and compare the interpretability of updates from NMT and its equivalent linguistic instruction-tuning method, known as Rule-Based Translation (RBT). Our analysis explores updates across three categories: human feedback, structural adjustments, and four distinct types of conceptual modifications. Our findings reveal that while both RBT and NMT effectively identify and correct update patterns involving feedback and syntax, they struggle with concepts related to politeness and vocabulary. Furthermore, we observe a significant disparity in how updates are handled; NMT frequently incorporates semantic alterations absent in the source text, whereas RBT functions more adherently to an editing paradigm. Finally, we investigate contextual variance, demonstrating that contextual homogeneity in NMT training data can lead to spurious interpretations of specific update patterns.

Recent laboratory experiments utilizing magnetic traps have detected signals consistent with the presence of fermionic dark matter possessing ultra-low masses ($m_{\rm DM} \sim 10^{-22}$--$10^{-16}$ GeV). We demonstrate that if such signals originate from classical axion fields within this specific mass range, the detectable interaction strengths would exceed current experimental sensitivity limits by many orders of magnitude. Consequently, successful observations in these magnetic trap searches effectively rule out ultra-light axions as the primary component of dark matter, provided that classicalization occurs on timescales shorter than approximately $10^{10}$ years.

Nuclear migration constitutes a fundamental process during the development of the C. elegans embryo, where nuclei move from the cortex to the center before cellular division. This study introduces a new mathematical model that accounts for the movement of nuclei and the dynamics of cell division. By applying this framework to experimental data, the paper analyzes how migration and division interact to drive the evolving population's behavior. The proposed methodology offers a general approach for analyzing cell and nucleus movement in both computational and experimental settings.

This paper introduces a novel class of two-dimensional (2D) structured sparse transforms, known as 2D Generalized Common Support (2D-GCS) transforms. These transforms enforce a strict geometric constraint where the non-zero pattern of the transform coefficients forms a shared geometric support across all pixels in an image. Consequently, the total number of non-zeros in the transform domain is limited to $(N - n)n$, with $N$ representing the total pixels and $n$ the size of the common support. Reconstruction algorithms are designed assuming the 2D-GCS transform matrix is orthogonal. The proposed family of 2D-GCS transforms includes the 2D Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) sparsity pattern enforced by Total Variation (TV) regularization and the 2D K-Singular Value decomposition (K-SVD) pattern with its specific common support constraint. To illustrate the effectiveness of these geometrically sparse representations, we define a new regularization term called "support cardinality" and integrate it into standard $l_2$-norm data fidelity. This yields a new regularization term: $J(X) = l_2\text{-norm}(W\text{-transform}(X)) + \text{support\_cardinality}(W\text{-transform}(X))$, which is then optimized for various applications, including denoising, deblurring, and compressed sensing.

Active systems, such as self-propelled particles, are known to generate long-range correlations driven by continuous energy consumption, a phenomenon often modeled within hydrodynamic frameworks. This study presents a new continuum theory for the Krauss-Parmentier defects in active nematics, challenging the standard view by revealing that system-wide correlation lengths increase at a $\sim t^2$ rate. This quadratic progression contrasts sharply with the $(n > 1)$ scaling predicted by linear hydrodynamic approaches. While the proposed model lacks full reversibility—accounting for particle motility without requiring their interactions—it successfully captures the leading-order dynamics observed in Krauss–Parmentier's original work across various dimensions. Specifically, under conditions of low particle density, the theory yields a $\sim t^2$ scaling for two and three dimensions, and produces only logarithmically slow growth for dimensions four and higher. Consequently, for any physical setup where the linear hydrodynamic regime does not apply, this framework offers a distinct mechanistic explanation for activity-induced long-range ordering that deviates from traditional predictions.

ID cards are critical documents for extracting personal details, and utilizing NLP to automate this extraction has become increasingly significant. However, variations in ID card layouts and text orientations often cause traditional methods to underperform. This paper introduces a robust approach for ID card text extraction that leverages the CACVD, a newly established and extensive dataset comprising 30,000 Vietnamese National Identity Cards. The CACVD features, such as diverse structures and multi-directional text, were incorporated into a state-of-the-art extraction algorithm. Experimental results indicate that this model significantly outperforms current leading methods, achieving a precision of 98.6% and recall of 97.9%.

This paper introduces a novel method for constructing time-dependent coherent states tailored to driven quantum systems, ensuring they adhere to exact Schrödinger dynamics. We focus on Hamiltonians featuring linear coupling between classical and quantum degrees of freedom—such as those describing polarons, spin-boson models, and Jaynes-Cummings systems. By employing these time-dependent coherent states as an ansatz within the Feynman path integral framework, we derive an effective action for the centroid that is non-Markovian yet strictly exact. Consequently, this effective action serves as an ideal foundation for partitioning the motion of the centroid into independent segments, thereby enabling the exact evaluation of path integrals for both propagators and operator expectations values. As a specific illustration, we consider a external force oscillating at a single frequency; in this scenario, the exact propagator and corresponding expectation values are obtained explicitly.

A report by Kowal et al. (2009) analyzed light curves of 2,163 asteroids from the Catalina Sky Survey, revealing a significant number—specifically 216—showed rotation rate increases. While the cause for this consistent acceleration in the same objects remains unclear, the potential role of solar radiation yarkovsky effect was examined using light curve data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). By compiling precise absolute magnitudes ($H$) and effective diameters ($D$) for these specific 216 high-priority asteroids, a sample-wide average spin lifetime against the radiation yarkovsky was derived. The results indicate that the median spin lifetime is significantly longer than the age of the solar system, leading to the conclusion that the phenomenon responsible for the observed spin-up cannot be the solar radiation yarkovsky effect for this population.

The work by Canny (1986) established that determining the rationality of a function $R(x,y)$ is computationally equivalent to deciding the non-emptiness of the semi-algebraic sets defined by such functions. Building on this, our paper presents an effective algorithm to decide whether a rational function $R(x,y)$ defines a continuous function on its domain of definition $\text{dom}(R) \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. This includes calculating the connected components of $\text{dom}(R)$ and identifying unbounded connected components in addition to finding all connected components within $\mathbb{R}^2$. We also extend these procedures to cases where the domain is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ for any $d \in \mathbb{N}$.

Reservoir computing (RC) demonstrates its ability to model complex systems, including systems characterized by multiple timescales and coexisting dynamical regimes. This study investigates the application of RC to address systems with significant variations in time scales, non-linear coexistence of states, and multistability. Our research identifies that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and various dynamical attractors within the RC structure function as crucial elements for managing these challenges and for accurately predicting system trajectories. We examine the intrinsic mechanisms of the RC architecture that facilitate these predictions and present several applications, including trajectory forecasting for a Lorenz-96 model with multiple timescales, a Langton ant moving on a lattice, and a system exhibiting a heteroclinic network. Additionally, we provide an in-depth look at forecasting a system driven by a heteroclinic network with an added chaotic attractor. Finally, we explore the existence of multistability within the RC itself and the requirement for appropriate initial conditions to successfully track specific system trajectories.

This paper introduces a method for computing feedback-controlled reachable states within a specific time horizon. The approach partitions continuous time into discrete steps, associating each step's control inputs with a zone (representing a parallelized set). State space exploration proceeds backward from final time to the initial point, utilizing the feedback control constraint to restrict reachable states within a corresponding zone. While prior research has addressed feedback-controlled past trajectories of fixed duration, this work uniquely handles variable-length trajectories. The time variability is encoded as zones, and the resulting union of feedback-controlled paths that satisfy these time bounds constitutes the ultimate reachable set. A significant advantage of this framework is its ability to incorporate non-differentiable constraints, such as those found in hybrid systems, by utilizing the parallelized zone data structure.

Our research establishes a significant strengthening of the condition for the non-existence of exceptional (Landau-Siegel) zeros within $\mathbb{Q}$-field automorphic L-functions of fixed weight $k \geq 2$ and central character $\psi$. This refinement builds upon previously work by Basset, which leveraged the repulsion phenomenon where L-function zeros move away from the critical line $\operatorname{Re}(s)=1/2$ when an exceptional zero is absent. In our approach, we re-examine Basset's framework utilizing the classical 1st moment of the Riemann zeta function instead of Ivić's estimate for that same critical moment. This substitution allows the "repulsion" effect to persist even when dealing with general Dirichlet characters $\psi$, extending beyond just those with trivial character.

Quantum relational Hoare logic (qRHL) serves as the foundational framework for establishing invariant relationships and relating initial and final states within programs, adapted specifically for quantum logic. Traditionally, the application of RHL is guided by a set of sound inference rules designed to reflect the invariant concepts found in classical relational RHL. However, this existing approach lacks the ability to support a fully automated derivation of judgments based on program input-output behavioral relationships. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel methodology for quantifying relationships between programs' inputs and outputs in the qRHL context. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces a framework for estimating these effects with robust inference that applies to both directed and undirected networks. The method addresses various identification challenges, including endogeneity, heterogeneity, and complex correlation structures within the error terms. A key innovation involves constructing a heteroskedasticity and endogeneity-robust error term that exhibits spatially varying properties across different parts of the network. This term enables the formation of cluster-variant spatially structured clusters for inference, effectively mitigating the issues caused internal error correlations. The proposed estimator offers practical advantages by requiring minimal assumptions regarding the density or specific form of external correlations, and it is validated through simulation studies and an empirical analysis of firm performance.

This study introduces and analyzes several classifications of chain rule formulas designed for variable-order fractional differentiation and integration. The associated variable orders must adhere to specific smoothness requirements, enabling the application of generalized L'Hôpital's rule within these chain rule formulations. The developed rules are validated across a range of variable-order fractional operators, including those defined by Riemann-Liouville, Caputo, and Hadamard. Furthermore, the paper examines the inversion of these chain rule formulas via fractional integrals of variable order. Key applications of these formulas are demonstrated, such as in the derivation of variable-order fractional versions of Taylor's formula and in the development of enhanced variable-order numerical methods for both Caputo and Riemann-Liouville differentiation.

This study investigates goal-oriented outcomes in cooperative games where two agents navigate a graph to reach distinct goals while facing stochastic obstacles. We analyze how varying levels of an opponent's complexity influence these success rates in a joint setting. By integrating the consideration of the adversary in multi-agent scenarios, we introduce a "theory of mind" capability for the collaborators. Our results demonstrate that anticipating and adapting to this strategic dynamic enhances achievement probabilities for both agents, even when the game is balanced so that neither holder an inherent advantage.

Protein knots are categorized by their folding kinetics into shallow and deep types, with the distinction based on kinetic barrier heights relative to those of unknotted homologs. This work introduces the concept of "topological frustration," defined as the ratio of the kinetic barrier specifically arising from knotting to the total kinetic barrier. We analyze this phenomenon using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations on proteins harboring the Figure-eight knot ($5_4$) and those containing a Figure-eight ($4_1$) knot. Our findings reveal that the folding trajectories for the Figure-eight ($5_4$) case—characterized kinetically as shallow—differ notably from those of the Figure-eight (4_1) [which is deeply knotted], despite sharing the same knot type. Specifically, while the Figure-eight (4_1) and the Figure-eight (5_4) show similar shallow pathways for distinct configurations, the barrier positions within the Figure-eight (4_1) folding pathway shift upon the conversion of the Figure-eight (4_1) to the Figure-eight (5_4). We conclude that these divergent shallow mechanisms stem from variations in the structural arrangement of the figure-eight knot.

We establish a result demonstrating the unicity (up to equivalence) of an irrationality condition on a symplectic form within a fixed symplectic manifold, given another symplectic form in the same class. In addition, an adjunction theory is developed that applies to both contact and symplectic structures.

We demonstrate that generating a mass for a Nambu-Goldstone (NG) boson within a standard Higgs-inclusive two-doublet model (Hi2DM)—where one doublet drives spontaneous symmetry breaking while the other remains unbroken—can be effectively modeled using kaon condensation. In this framework, the NG boson corresponds to a "kaon," the other Hi2DM doublet acts as the analogue of the "anti-kaon," and the Higgs field plays the role of the "$\pi$-meson." We derive the specific parameter space required within the two-dimensions of the Hi2DM to replicate the physical characteristics of real kaon condensation. We also examine the extension involving mass terms that distinguish between particles and antiparticles, noting how such terms prevent the symmetry from breaking and thereby prevent the NG boson from acquiring mass. Finally, we analyze a variant where this particle-antiparticle asymmetry is dynamic rather than explicit; in this scenario, the Hi2DM parameters must satisfy specific constraints to allow the "asymmetric" phase to emerge as a minimum of the effective potential, positioning it at the same energy level as the standard symmetric minimum.

We investigate the impact of practicing with counterfactual data, produced via our novel method, on both robustness and generalization. DISCO, which stands for Discontinuous Landscape Disco, efficiently generates diverse, fact-based training data by strategically navigating a training set's decision boundaries to discover and move across them. Experiments reveal that models trained using DISCO-tailored data significantly improve generalization and robustness compared to those trained only on original datasets. We observe that the enhancement in generalization increases exponentially as the volume of DISCO-generated data grows, whereas the improvement in robustness follows a distinct pattern. Finally, we analyze the underlying mechanisms driving these results, highlighting how the strategic placement of data points influences the final model's behavior.

The epitaxial growth of materials on graphene substrates offers a pathway to achieve atomic cleanliness and electrical isolation, yet the resulting structural phase and domain composition are dictated by the specific material and growth parameters. This study reveals a temperature-dependent evolution in the formation of different epitaxial domains within the $\text{La}_2\text{NiO}_4/\text{Graphene}$ system. Scanning tunneling microscopy indicates that growth at lower temperatures favors the formation of the $(2\times 2)$-domain, characterized by Ni atoms positioned directly above graphene carbon atoms, whereas higher temperatures promote the $(\sqrt{3}\times 1)$-domain. Furthermore, while the fundamental unit cells of these domains remain stable, their relative lattice constants exhibit a thermal expansion behavior distinct from that of bulk material. These findings were validated through density functional theory calculations, which also account for the role of interfacial strain and substrate-induced modifications in dictating the preferred growth domains.

This study examines the specific ranges for the 1 to 12 coefficients of a mixed Z_3 and Z_9-linear code, establishing the limits on their possible values. The various scenarios are analyzed to determine the minimum possible rank, with the findings used to reconstruct a wide variety of these lines of code with high rank. Finally, the process concludes with the building of mixed lines with the maximal rank using these results.

Existing multi-label datasets are scarce, necessitating the reuse of single-label data through conversion methods. However, current Single-to-Multi-label (S2M) approaches often generate implausible additional labels, as their typical use of top-k sampling based on predicted probabilities fails to ensure diversity and frequently results in label sets that are mutually exclusive. To resolve this, we propose a supervised framework for creating high-quality multi-label datasets from single-label pairs using our novel S2M strategy, termed "Closed-Loop S2M with Optimized Label Selection" (S2M-OLS). This approach leverages an active learning cycle to gather multi-label examples, which are then employed to train a model capable of guiding further single-label to multi-expansions. The efficacy of the resulting multi-label data is validated across various downstream tasks, demonstrating marked improvements when compared to multi-label sets constructed via standard S2M techniques.

We introduce the concept of a *weakly natural* transformation, defined as a functor that is both functorial and universal in an appropriate categorical sense. We demonstrate that this notion serves as a universal, functorial extension of natural transformations and establishes a fully categorical framework for analyzing their adjunction properties. Furthermore, we develop a general theory of "two-sided" weak naturality that encompasses "fully weak" weak naturality as a specific instance; this specific case provides a universal and functorial setting for analyzing the universal properties of adjunctions themselves.

The discrepancy between Fermi and ground-based Cherenkov telescopes regarding GeV excess emission toward the Galactic Center has prompted the proposal of the MAG and MAD models. These frameworks attribute the puzzle to the suppression of GeV pion-driven gamma rays, caused by electrons heated to non-thermal levels that emit GeV radiation via inverse Compton scattering off intense infrared and optical photons near the Galactic Center. This study presents a revised formulation of the MAD model, incorporating more realistic assumptions regarding the cosmic ray reference spectrum, cosmic ray transport mechanisms, and electron cooling processes. Our results demonstrate that while the updated model effectively explains the observed TeV data, its ability to account for the GeV excess is diminished unless the electron heating rate is significantly elevated. Consequently, stronger heating is required in the regions generating pion-mediated gamma rays than was originally assumed in the MAD framework.

Cardiovascular diseases represent a significant global health challenge, with early diagnosis being critical for effective management. Although electrocardiograms (ECGs) are a standard tool for identifying heart conditions, their utility is often hindered by background noise and various artifacts. To address these challenges, this study introduces a framework for automated ECG signal classification that integrates an attention mechanism into a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) architecture. This model is designed to extract both the salient features and intricate patterns inherent in ECG data. Furthermore, the study proposes a novel data augmentation strategy utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to boost the efficacy of the attention-CNN-LSTM classifier. The proposed solution was evaluated on the MIT-Beat dataset, demonstrating a 98.98\% accuracy rate. These findings indicate that the combination of the gan-augmented attention-CNN-LSTM approach offers a robust solution for the automatic classification of arrhythmias within ECG signals.

Individualized activity patterns are a well-known limitation in wearable activity recognition, a challenge that grows more significant as the variety of detectable human actions expands. Achieving high accuracy for these learnable models typically requires frequent, intrusive retraining, which hinders the practical deployment of wearable systems. To address this, we introduce FedHealth, a framework that unites private, real-time federated fine-tuning directly on user devices. This approach enables precise activity recognition by adapting shared neural network models to individual habits, all while maintaining data privacy and requiring no internet connection. FedHealth integrates two key innovations: first, an efficient mechanism for updating local model parameters using private data without full training cycles, and second, a privacy-preserving update selection strategy that ensures only high-quality contributions are aggregated. We validated FedHealth across two distinct studies involving 100 participants and 10 different wearable activity classes. The results demonstrate that the system achieves real-time, accurate recognition of user-specific activities, significantly surpassing both traditional methods and existing federated learning benchmarks in its ability to adapt to personalization.

This study introduces a hybrid multi-objective optimization framework designed to enhance the performance of utility optimization strategies for investment portfolios. The core methodology involves transforming non-linear objective functions and their associated constraints into an extensive multi-dimensional objective space. Within this space, the EliashbergEversheim (EE) algorithm performs a multi-objective optimization process to generate a new set of weighted objectives that effectively re-negotiates trade-offs. These dynamic weights are derived from the gradient directions typical of utility maximization. Applied to the efficient frontier analysis of an illiquid stock portfolio, results demonstrate that the proposed multi-objective approach outperforms standard single- and multi-criterion methods by more accurately aligning optimal outcomes with specific utility functions.

The recruitment of talent typically involves scheduling numerous interviews, a process where automation can significantly reduce administrative burdens. A critical component of algorithmic scheduling involves forming interview panels, which consists of selecting committee members and determining their availability. In this study, we introduce a novel algorithmic framework for assembling an interview committee. We model the problem using a utility function designed to optimize committee composition by balancing the total candidate load against committee diversity. Additionally, we define a specific method for scoring the diversity of individual panelists based on their department, research interests, and gender. Our approach incorporates an algorithm that generates diverse committees by balancing these competing objectives. We validate our model and solution using data from a real-world recruitment event and conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the impact of diversity scoring and the variety of available diversity measures.

This study examines the leading-order hadronic scattering processes generating lequark pairs at proton colliders. We systematically organize the corresponding Feynman diagrams into distinct categories based on the applicability of decoupling and enhanced effects, thereby clarifying the production mechanisms across a broad spectrum of energy scales. Specifically, we assess asymmetric lequark pair production, concluding that it demands both enhanced symmetry breaking effects and a mass suppression relative to lequarks to achieve significant contributions. Finally, we extend our analysis to the associated production of scalar lequarks with pseudoscalar lequark pairs.

Recent Hubble and Spitzer observations have identified a class of extreme galaxies characterized by stellar formation rates exceeding 1,000 solar masses per year. While the driving mechanisms for such bursts remain debated, a significant controversy exists regarding the kinematics of CO lines in these systems: specifically, whether they reflect a low-density molecular outflow or access to a circumgalactic gas reservoir. This study analyzes the spectral line ratios from [CI] (1-0), (2-1), and (3-2) transitions in eight extreme galaxies to investigate this issue. The results indicate that the [CI] (2-0.5) and (1.5) emission ratios—calculated from the (2-1) and (3-2) lines—are significantly elevated compared to standard local universe values. These discrepancies are too substantial to result from optical depth variations or simple non-LTE effects alone. We demonstrate that the most plausible explanation involves a low-density wind or outflow, which shifts the excitation conditions of the [CI] (2-1) line toward a two-level system while minimally affecting other lines. Consequently, the (2-0.5) and (1.5) ratios serve as powerful diagnostic tools for identifying extreme galaxy outflows. Furthermore, the magnitude of these deviations allows for the estimation of the velocity dispersion within the molecular wind.

This study analyzes the velocity distribution $t$ for a second-class ASES particle within an asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) starting from step. As time progresses, two distinct temporal regimes emerge: in the short-term limit ($t \ll N$), the distribution aligns with that of the GOE universality class, whereas for extended durations ($t \gg N$), it conforms to the diagonalized Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (dGOE) universality class. We offer a comprehensive description of the transition between these two regimes and derive the mathematical framework characterizing the intermediate timescale when $t \sim N$.

In the analysis of time-series data governed by differential models, a prevalent methodology involves defining a cost function as the discrepancy between model predictions and observed data, which is subsequently optimized regarding model parameters. While effective, this approach has a notable shortcoming: it disregards whether trajectories generated by the model are biologically realistic. To address this limitation, we propose an alternative strategy that integrates biologically meaningful constraints directly into the objective function. Specifically, for the application of SIR (Susceptible, Infected, Recovered) models to epidemiological datasets, this paper demonstrates the formulation of a new cost function. This function combines three distinct components: the alignment with historical data, adherence to non-negative parameter requirements, and the enforcement of biological bounds inherent to the SIR differential equations themselves. To illustrate the efficacy of this methodology, we apply it to analyze COVID-19 case data concerning Mexico.

A quantum system comprising mixed atoms and molecules is investigated, with a specific focus on the conditions triggering atom-molecule instability and the subsequent cascade collapse. The atom fraction undergoing conversion is mapped to explore these phenomena, a process characterized by a non-rigid pendulum effective model. This framework clarifies both the mechanisms of conversion and collapse dynamics, predicting a universal scaling law for the atom fraction required to initiate instability. Furthermore, the hysteresis inherent in conversion dynamics is identified as a diagnostic signature confirming collapse. Within this quantum non-rigid pendulum context, a distinct class of coherent atom-molecule oscillations is discovered, where the mean atom fraction fluctuates between two distinct values.

In DNA data storage, organizing DNA molecules into distinct storage partitions, controlled by specific primer pairs, is essential for efficient information management. A significant challenge in this domain is creating primer sets that minimize costly biochemical operations such as encoding, erasure, and replication. This study introduces a novel methodology and optimization framework for designing these primers to enhance storage overhead. The approach models the storage protocol as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and incorporates optimization criteria focused on reducing operational costs. We developed a linear function approximation algorithm to solve this MDP, yielding time-independent optimization parameters. Simulations demonstrate that for storage operations like erasure and erasure-complement, the proposed technique lowers total overhead by 11% and 13% respectively compared to current state-of-the-art methods, with performance improving as the number of storage partitions increases.

This study introduces a novel Principal Component Geostatistical Approach (PCGA) designed to estimate riverbed bathymetry using sparse LiDAR velocity data. The method integrates Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with geostatistics to model the spatial patterns of the PCA components derived from existing velocity data points. By combining these geostatistically estimated components with PCA weights extracted from high-resolution multibeam sonar (MBES) data, the PCGA effectively reconstructs flow velocities across the entire cross-section. Consequently, standard single- and multi-point profiling techniques can generate continuous velocity distributions, enabling the accurate inference of bed elevation. Validation against the standard cross-correlation of before-and-after MBES datasets confirms the approach's efficacy. Specifically, when applied to a case involving 11 velocity profiles, the PCGA yielded a root mean square error (RMSE) in elevation estimation of 0.07 meters, representing a 93% reduction compared to traditional methods.

High Dynamic Range (HDR) acquisition is critical for accurately rendering scenes with extreme brightness variations. While HDR techniques rely on combining multiple frames taken with different exposure times, the efficacy of tone mapping hinges on automatically selecting these exposure times. Traditionally, this selection process has been handled manually, a drawback that Automatic Exposure Setting Selection (AESS) aims to rectify. Although AESS methods have been developed, they are rarely utilized in current hardware due to constraints such as limited buffer memory, processing latency, and reduced roll-off performance in dark areas. This study introduces an AESS approach designed for embedded systems that overcomes these specific hardware limitations. The proposed method utilizes a histogram-based exposure algorithm optimized for both speed and accuracy. Furthermore, it incorporates a novel mechanism to ensure frame-to-frame exposure consistency, thereby eliminating visible artifacts caused by fluctuating exposure levels. The authors report the implementation details, including the algorithm's execution on an embedded platform, along with its quantitative and qualitative assessment when compared against manual setting methods.

We examine the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner for the steady-state Stokes problem featuring homogeneous Dirichlet conditions on a subdomain. Our investigation into a periodic setting introduces several novel aspects: the definition of primal degrees of freedom now encompasses both standard node-based and face-based edge variables from the velocity field, as well as scalar variables representing the normal component on a cocycle from the pressure field; the analysis allows for non-uniform, general mesh configurations; and it addresses strong scaling on a powerful supercomputer system using the FEniCS software framework for discretization. In this context, we specify distinct definitions for both the local and global degrees of freedom within the multilevel H^1(FE) space. The study establishes that the BDDC complexity relies polynomially on the finite element polynomial degree and only logarithmically on both the period of the problem and the size of the strong scaling test. It is also important to note the specific selection of both the primal decompositions and the auxiliary space employed within this setup.

We demonstrate that introducing correlations and heterogeneity into the initial conditions of a standard Gaussian diffusion model can result in a non-Gaussian dynamical system. Within this specific framework, the resulting distribution remains invariant under the transformation where time and the diffusion coefficient are swapped. Consequently, the diffusion coefficient must exhibit a strong, heterogeneous dependence on position to generate non-Gaussian behavior. Finally, we analyze the connections between our findings and recent experimental data regarding DNA transport in micro- and nano-fluidic environments under low Reynolds number conditions.

We present an analytical and numerical analysis of nonlinear effects within the fundamental mode of an laser resonator, specifically examining interactions between co- and counterpropagating waves. Our investigation calculates mode coupling coefficients and nonlinear coupling coefficients to determine the conditions for cross-phase modulation and self-phase modulation. Results indicate that for the identical fundamental mode pairing, nonlinear self-phase modulation in one direction is roughly ten times more intense than the neutralizing cross-phase modulation exerted by the opposite direction. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the Q-factor of the highly reflective single direction and explore how group-velocity mismatch influences the phase dynamics. As a practical application, we utilize these models to analyze the frequency-shifting capabilities of a residential fiber optic loop, demonstrating a net 30-MHz increase using 50-ps pulses at 1500 nm.

This study introduces a novel application of a multiscale enhanced super-resolution Generative Adversarial Network (MSER-SR GAN) to reconstruct full-velocity fields from coarse-resolution Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) data across a spectrum of varying Stokes flow and turbulent channel conditions. By analyzing both laminar and turbulent regimes, the model demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional super-resolution methods when improving low Reynolds number (Stokes) flows through minor image details through multi-scale image enhancement. For turbulent channel flow, the model improves super-resolution by integrating multi-scale features and prior information from realistic images without any training on physical laws or synthetic data related to the specific problem setup or boundary conditions. Specifically, in the laminar case, results indicate a strong correlation where increased input image sharpness—achieved through increased Stokes flow parameters—results in more accurate velocity reconstructions relative to ground truth results. Similarly, in the turbulent scenario, increased intensity in scoring mechanisms (related to chaos) also improves accuracy of the velocity field reconstruction relative to other methods. Ultimately, the utilization of increased scoring mechanisms and multi-scale feature integration allows this method to effectively handle various physical regimes, including those characterized by high chaos levels and complex dynamics.

To assess the curricular effects within algorithmic problem difficulty adjustment, this study introduces a controlled modification strategy for the Ant environment (Garcia & Hayes, 2024). We propose a gradual escalation of block probabilities in the standard curriculum, offering a flexible alternative to the original curricular approach. Our findings demonstrate that these targeted adjustments yield performance outcomes nearly identical to those of the original curriculum. Furthermore, these adjustments prove effective for evaluating both the gradient-based methods (specifically PPO) and an eligibility-tracing-based off-policy algorithm (TD-errors), confirming their utility as a benchmarking framework. This modular design not only facilitates rigorous algorithmic assessment but also provides a simplified setup for investigating curriculum learning phenomena.

Dr. graphs (DCR graphs) model the evolution of business processes by representing distinct workflows and their shifts. While existing DCR graph evolution frameworks are effective for analyzing changes between two states, they fall short when applied to dynamic, real-time business environments. In such active scenarios, incorporating new activities, altering current behaviors, or adjusting constraints is necessary to sustain an accurate model of process behavior changes over time. To address this, we introduce a live DCR graph concept that functions as an evolving model capable of accounting for these temporal shifts. We define specific operations to facilitate the required updates, including methods to introduce new activities, modify transitions between activities, and adjust constraints. We also present an algorithm that utilizes these updates to integrate new observable traces, thereby keeping the graph aligned with actual behavior. The significance of this "liveness" in facilitating accurate, ongoing model maintenance through the addition of traces from business-as-us operations is highlighted.
